title: LZ78 compression and decompression
label: idb
statement: **Reconstructed — the original statement was not recovered.** Implement LZ78: `Encode` turns a string into tokens `(Index, Next)`, where `Index` is the dictionary number of the longest previously-seen phrase that prefixes the rest of the input (0 = empty phrase) and `Next` is the following character; that phrase+char becomes the next dictionary entry. If the input ends exactly on a known phrase, the final token's `Next` is `'\0'`. `Decode` reverses it.
provenance: Title from the InterviewDB list; the statement was not recovered (searches found no public LinkedIn reference). **This is a reconstruction**: the LZ78 algorithm (Lempel & Ziv, 1978) is standard and certain; the token format and API below are my choice, not the interviewer's. Clarify the format first if you meet it for real.

stages.title: Encode and decode
stages.say: Implement LZ78 compression and decompression. Tell me the token format you will use before you start.
stages.require: Implement `Lz78.Encode(s)` and `Lz78.Decode(tokens)`. Null or empty → no tokens / empty string.
testNames: input ending on a known phrase: last token is (1, '\\0')

stages.title: Bounded memory
stages.say: The input is a multi-gigabyte log. Your dictionary grows forever. Bound it.
stages.require: Add an optional `maxEntries` parameter to both: `Encode(s, maxEntries)` and `Decode(tokens, maxEntries)`. When the dictionary is full, reset it — and both sides must reset at the same token.
testNames: bounded round trips for maxEntries 1, 2, 5, 50; no index exceeds the bound

flaw.ctx: You asked for the LZ78 decoder.
flaw.answer: Phrases are numbered from 1 but stored from list index 0, so `phrases[index]` reads the **next** phrase — or throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for the newest one. The comment states the right convention and the code contradicts it; that is exactly the kind of line to read rather than trust.
flaw.fix: `phrases[index - 1]` — or seed the list with `""` at index 0 as the reference does.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- What is the token format — (index, char) pairs, or a byte stream? (Here: pairs.)
- What happens when the input ends in the middle of a known phrase?
- Is the dictionary bounded? (Stage 2.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Encoder and decoder grow the same dictionary in the same order, so the dictionary never has to be transmitted. Everything rests on that symmetry — including the bounded-memory follow-up, where both sides must reset at exactly the same token.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "A." Dictionary<string,int> of phrases seen so far, extended one character at a time while the prefix is known, emits (index of longest known phrase, next char) — and the decoder rebuilds the same phrase list from the tokens."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Off-by-one between 0 = empty phrase and 1-based dictionary numbers.
- Dropping the trailing phrase when input ends on a known phrase.
- An encoder and decoder that reset a bounded dictionary at different moments.
- Building every substring with `Substring` in a hot loop on large input (allocation-heavy — a trie fixes it).

**Verification exercise:** Off-by-one — Phrases are numbered from 1 but stored from list index 0, so `phrases[index]` reads the **next** phrase — or throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for the newest one. The comment states the right convention and the code contradicts it; that is exactly the kind of line to read rather than trust.
